sentences.text: Species of Mekosuchus were generally small, terrestrial crocodilians under 2 meters long with short, blunt snouts and strong limbs.
Mekosuchus had a short and raised skull shape, unlike the elongated and flattened skulls of most modern crocodiles.
Mekosuchus possessed large eye sockets that were partially formed by the maxilla bone, a feature unique among crocodilians.
Mekosuchus displayed a wave-like arrangement of teeth in the jaw known as festooning.
The eyes and nostrils of Mekosuchus were not adapted for an aquatic lifestyle.
The first fossil bone of Mekosuchus, a fragmentary quadratojugal, was collected from Kanumera Bay in New Caledonia in 1981.
Fossils of Mekosuchus were first reported by Eric Buffetaut in 1983 and formally described by him and Jean-Christophe Balouet in 1987.
The species M. whitehunterensis was described by Paul Willis in 1997 from fossils found at the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland.
The species M. kalpokasi was named in 2002 from fragmentary remains found at an archaeological site on Vanuatu.
Some researchers suggest that Mekosuchus species were nocturnal and lived near rainforest streams.
Despite its small size, Mekosuchus likely possessed strong neck muscles based on its vertebrae structure.
Both Mekosuchus inexpectatus and M. whitehunterensis had an overbite where upper teeth covered lower teeth.
The genus Mekosuchus was described by Balouet and Buffetaut in 1987.
Balouet and Buffetaut classified Mekosuchus as a Eusuchian and placed it in the family Mekosuchidae based on choanae and procoelous vertebrae.
Research has expanded the family to include many other taxa, and it is now referred to as Mekosuchinae.
Willis (1997) suggested a close link between Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus, with Quinkana as their sister taxon.
The earliest members of Mekosuchus lived in mainland Australia during the Oligocene and Miocene epochs.
Mekosuchus likely went extinct around 3,000 years ago during the Holocene, though some authors suggest it survived longer.
Radiocarbon dating suggests M. inexpectatus fossils from the Isle of Pines date to approximately 3,750 years before present.
Some M. inexpectatus fossils from the Pindai Caves may date to approximately 1,720 years before present.
It is debated whether human activity caused the extinction of Mekosuchus, as no direct evidence of human involvement has been found despite suggestions of a human cause.
Holt and colleagues suggest that M. kalpokasi may be synonymous with M. inexpectatus due to poor preservation and overlapping geographic and temporal ranges.
Mead and colleagues argue that continental drift did not cause the appearance of mekosuchines in the South Pacific.
It is possible that mekosuchines dispersed by actively swimming or drifting on natural rafts, though this is not confirmed.
